data.title: The Cartographer's Apprentice
data.summary: A young mapmaker gets an impossible job: to draw a place that does not exist yet. A story about maps, mistakes and the difference between measuring and understanding.
data.author: The Cartilla Sessions
data.intro: In the map workshop on Aldana Street, every map was drawn by hand and every mistake was fixed in red ink. At seventeen, Nilo believed that fixing mistakes was the only way to draw well.

chapters.title: The workshop on Aldana Street
paragraphs: The workshop smelled of ink and paper that had dried too many times. Nilo's master, Doña Irene, had drawn coastlines for forty years, and she kept every rejected sheet in a drawer that nobody was allowed to open.
"A map is an argument," she told him on his first morning. "Somebody looked at the world and decided what was worth keeping. Your job is to make a better argument."

Nilo copied coastlines for a year. He learned how to let a line curve without trembling, how to space a letter so a name would fit on a narrow peninsula, how to leave white space where a mountain should go. He was good at it. He never asked what the white space was for.

In the second year, Doña Irene gave him a commission that the other apprentices refused. "The valley of the river Arupi," she said, "nobody has surveyed. It flooded last winter and the old map is wrong. Go and look."

chapters.title: What the flood changed
paragraphs: The river had moved. That was the first fact, and it was enough to ruin a month of the old map. Where there had been a bend there was now a straight cut, and where there had been a grove of willows there was a shallow lake full of branches.

Nilo measured the new course twice, carefully, because he wanted the number to be right. Then he walked upstream to the village of Puerto Alegre, because that was on the old map and he needed to check whether the road still reached the river.

It did not. The road had ended in a cliff of mud forty metres from the water. The people of Puerto Alegre had been walking to a different landing place for eleven months. No one had thought to send word to the workshop.

"So we redraw it," Nilo said to himself, and opened his notebook to write the new road. Then he stopped, because he had no idea what the villagers called the place where they now crossed. It was not on any map. It was, he realised, not a place yet. It was a habit.

chapters.title: The argument
paragraphs: He stayed four more days. He sat in the school yard while the children showed him the stones they skipped at the new crossing, and he learned that the crossing was called *el paso de la abuela*, because the women of the village had crossed there so many times that nobody remembered when it started.

He drew the new river as it was. He drew the road as it was, ending in mud. And in the margin, in smaller letters than the rest, he wrote: *el paso de la abuela* — and marked it with a small square, the cartographers' sign for a place named by the people who live there.
Doña Irene read the sheet for a long time. Then she opened the drawer of rejected maps, took out thirty years of her own discarded sheets, and laid them on the table beside Nilo's.

"Every one of these is wrong," she said. "And every one of them was more useful than a perfect one, because someone trusted it enough to walk there." She put her finger on his margin. "You drew a river. Now you have drawn a road. This square you added is the first true thing on the map."
Nilo never became a famous cartographer. He became a better one. He learned that measuring is the easy half, and that the hard half is knowing which measurements matter enough to write down.

data.title: Letters from the Salt Road
data.summary: For thirty years, a woman wrote letters to her sister and never sent them. When she finally decides to send them, she finds that the letters no longer say what she thought.
data.author: The Cartilla Sessions
data.intro: Elena wrote her first letter at seventeen and did not send it. She wrote almost every week for thirty years and kept the letters in a banana box. When she finally decided to send them, she was no longer the person who wrote them.

chapters.title: The box under the bed
paragraphs: The letters were written on the backs of the delivery calendars from the shop on the corner, because paper cost money and Elena's mother kept the calendars to wrap things in. She had never thought of this as a habit. It was only that there was always a calendar, and there was always something to say.

In 1994 she wrote: *Mara, today a man came to the house to ask for my hand and I said no. I do not know why I said no. Write and tell me if that was foolish.* She never sent it. By the time she was ready to send it, six months had passed and the question had become strange.

By the year twenty she had filled two boxes. The first one, she remembered, held the years when she still believed she would send them. The second held the years when sending them had become a way of talking about herself.

chapters.title: The road
paragraphs: Mara had gone north in 1991 to work on the salt road, the one that runs flat along the edge of the flats, where the only landmarks are the piles of white that mark where the water has been taken out. Elena stayed in the town, married, divorced, kept the shop for six years, and then did not.

They wrote to each other. That is what Elena told people, and it was true, but not in the way it sounded. Mara's letters came every month, warm and funny and full of small news about weather and salt and a dog called Reglamento. Elena's letters did not come. Elena's letters went into the box.

What Elena did write, in those years, is the thing she could not say aloud: that she was lonely, that she had chosen wrong, that she thought about the road more than she thought about her husband. She wrote it beautifully. She wrote it so well that reading it back felt like reading about somebody else.

chapters.title: What the letters said
paragraphs: She took them out in the order she had written them, which was not the order she wanted to read them in. The first ones were so eager that they embarrassed her. The middle ones were so careful. And the last ones, the ones from the year thirty, were three pages long and full of a tenderness she could barely recognise, addressed to a woman she had become certain she would never be.

Mara was dead since the March. Elena had known that for two years and had not opened the box, because opening it would mean the last letter had no answer, and Elena had spent her life making sure that no letter of hers was without one.

In the end she did not send them. She drove north to the salt road with the two boxes in the boot of the car and she read them all there, in the flat white light, one after the other, out loud, to nobody. Then she drove back. The letters went back in the box under the bed, and this time she put the box on the shelf in the front room, in the light, where she could see it.
She did not need them to arrive. She had needed to know what she had said.

data.title: The Night the River Froze
data.summary: The shortest and easiest story here: a boy sees the river freeze for the first time and decides to cross it. Words about weather, cold and surprise.
data.author: The Cartilla Sessions
data.intro: Tomás had been told the river never froze. He had lived on its bank for eleven years and had only ever seen it move.

chapters.title: Thursday
paragraphs: On Thursday night the air was so still that the dogs did not bark. Tomás woke because the house was cold in a new way, and because he heard a sound he had never heard before: a long, thin crack, like a plate breaking in another room.
He went to the window. The river was white. Not white the way clouds are white, but white the way metal is white, and it was making that sound all along its length, from the bridge to the bend.
His father said the river had frozen like this once before, when Tomás was four. His mother said it had not. They agreed about nothing else that morning, which was normal.

chapters.title: The crossing
paragraphs: In the afternoon Tomás took his father's old skates and walked down to the bank. The ice was covered in a thin layer of snow, and where his foot landed the snow went under and the ice made a deep green sound under it, like a door.

He stepped out. The first step was frightening. The second was not. By the tenth he was laughing, and the laugh came out of him in the way that things come out of you when you are completely cold and completely happy at once.

Halfway across he stopped. The ice was thinner there, and he could see the black water moving under it, slow, carrying a leaf. He sat down on the ice immediately, because his legs had decided before he did, and he watched the leaf go.

When he got back his mother wrapped him in three blankets and asked him what he had seen. He said: "A leaf." She said: "You went onto the ice?" He said: "There's a leaf under the ice, and it's going to the sea." That was the answer he had prepared on the way home, and he delivered it with enormous seriousness, and both of his parents laughed, and he understood then that he had got away with it.

glossary.definition: To do something wrong without being caught or punished.

data.title: How to shadow a song
data.summary: The first episode: why singing along to an English song works better than repeating it in silence, and how to do shadowing in five steps that take fifteen minutes.

segments.speaker: Nina
segments.text: Welcome to The Practice Room. I'm Nina. Today we are going to do something that looks lazy and is not: we are going to sing along with a song in English, badly, and that is the point.

segments.speaker: Nina
segments.text: Most learners try to understand a song first. They listen, they look up every word, they try to translate the whole thing, and by the time they have understood it, they have lost the thread. Understanding a song is not the first step. Singing it is.

segments.speaker: Nina
segments.text: Here is the method. Five steps, fifteen minutes. First, listen once without the text. Just hear the shape of it. Notice where the music goes up and where it comes down.

segments.speaker: Nina
segments.text: Second, read the lyrics with your finger under the line. Not out loud yet. Your eye needs to find the lines first, because your mouth is going to have to find them later.

segments.speaker: Nina
segments.text: Third, sing. Badly. Nobody is listening. You are not singing for accuracy, you are singing for timing. You are training your mouth to arrive at the same moment as the singer.

segments.speaker: Nina
segments.text: Fourth, shadow. Now you follow the voice in real time, half a word behind, like a shadow. This is the hard part and it is the useful part. It trains your ear and your mouth at the same time.

segments.speaker: Nina
segments.text: And fifth, one line only. Pick the single line you liked best and sing it ten times until it is yours. Not the song. The line.

segments.speaker: Nina
segments.text: That is the whole method. Notice what is not in it: no dictionary, no grammar, no app that tells you your pronunciation was wrong. You need about fifteen minutes and a song you already like.

segments.speaker: Nina
segments.text: Try it now with Counting the Miles. Start with the first step: one listen, no text. Then come back and tell me how it went.

keyTerms.definition: Repeating what a speaker says a fraction of a second after them, to practise rhythm and pronunciation together.
keyTerms.example: Shadowing is the technique used in this episode.

keyTerms.definition: To reach a place or a moment, especially in time.
keyTerms.example: Your mouth must arrive at the word with the music.

keyTerms.definition: The general contour of a piece of music, which rises and falls.
keyTerms.example: Listen for the shape of the song before the words.

keyTerms.definition: One row of words in a song, between two musical phrases.
keyTerms.example: She sang one line of the chorus over and over.

comprehension.explanation: The episode says understanding a song is not the first step. Singing it is.

options: To sing the song correctly from the first try.

comprehension.explanation: Nina says: “You are singing for timing. You are training your mouth to arrive at the same moment as the singer.”

comprehension.explanation: “It trains your ear and your mouth at the same time.”

data.title: How coffee tastes of where it grows
data.summary: An episode about the story of coffee: why the taste of a cup depends on how high it grows, the weather and the hands that pick it, told from a farm in Colombia's coffee region.

segments.speaker: Lucía
segments.text: Hello, and welcome to El Sonido del Café. I'm Lucía, and today we are going to taste a place without tasting it. We are going to talk about how a coffee bean can taste of the hill it grew on.

segments.speaker: Lucía
segments.text: Picture a farm in the coffee-growing region of Colombia. The farm is not flat. It is a set of steep green slopes, and at the top of each slope the temperature is a little cooler than at the bottom.

segments.speaker: Lucía
segments.text: That difference of a few degrees is enough to change the bean. The cold nights slow the ripening, so the seed inside stays small and sweet, and the fruit around it turns a deep red. Those red fruits are called cherries, even though they are not fruit at all.

segments.speaker: Lucía
segments.text: Now the harvest. In Colombia most coffee is picked by hand, and this is not nostalgia. A machine can strip a branch in two seconds, but it takes the ripe cherries and the green ones together.

segments.speaker: Lucía
segments.text: So pickers walk the rows, and they look. They look for the colour, they feel the weight, and they take only what is right. A good picker can pick about sixty kilos of cherries in a day, and they can tell you the name of every farm on the slope.

segments.speaker: Lucía
segments.text: That name matters. Single-origin coffee is not a marketing word invented last year. It is an old promise: this cup came from this farm, this family, this hillside, in this year.

segments.speaker: Lucía
segments.text: And the last thing is the drying. The beans leave the farm as mucilage, a sticky layer like honey, and they are dried on patios or in parabolic beds under the sun for up to two weeks.

segments.speaker: Lucía
segments.text: During that time, whoever turns the beans is making decisions. Too much sun and they bake. Too little and they mould. A good worker reads the humidity in the afternoon and decides how thick to spread the layer.

segments.speaker: Lucía
segments.text: So when you drink a coffee that tastes of chocolate, or of orange, or of nothing in particular, none of that happened in your kitchen. It happened on a slope, in a season, in the hands of somebody you will never meet.

data.title: Working in a loud place
data.summary: An episode about noise: why busy, open rooms help some people focus and make it hard for others, and what to do when you cannot move somewhere quieter.

segments.speaker: Nina
segments.text: This is episode two of The Practice Room, and today we are talking about noise, which is either the best thing that has ever happened to your focus or the worst.

segments.speaker: Nina
segments.text: There is a well-known experiment from the nineties about this. Two groups of people did the same task. One group worked in silence and one worked with noise. The noisy group performed better on dull tasks and much worse on tasks that needed thought.

segments.speaker: Nina
segments.text: That is the whole story, really. Noise is not good or bad for your brain. It is good for one kind of work and terrible for another, and the mistake is using the wrong tool for the job.

segments.speaker: Nina
segments.text: So if you are doing something repetitive, something mechanical, something where your hands are busy and the decision-making is small, then background noise can carry you a long way. The music becomes a rhythm for the hands.

segments.speaker: Nina
segments.text: But if you are writing an argument, learning a language, or reading something you do not fully understand, then noise eats the part of your attention that holds the sentence in place. You read the line three times and still lose it at the end.

segments.speaker: Nina
segments.text: Here is what works if you cannot change your room. First, separate the noise from the task with headphones. Even headphones with no music playing will cut the sharp edges, and you can use the music at a volume low enough to disappear.

segments.speaker: Nina
segments.text: Second, give the hard task a fixed place and a fixed time. People protect what has a slot in the calendar much better than what is supposed to happen whenever there is a gap.

segments.speaker: Nina
segments.text: And third, keep one sound for one kind of work. If the same music plays while you write and while you rest, you stop learning what it means. Give the studying its own sound and the resting its own silence.

keyTerms.definition: A task that needs attention but little thought.
keyTerms.example: Folding laundry is a dull task.

keyTerms.definition: To use up a resource such as attention, so that less of it remains.
keyTerms.example: Background noise eats the attention needed to hold a sentence.

keyTerms.definition: An empty period of time between other commitments.
keyTerms.example: Studying in whatever gap appears rarely works.

keyTerms.definition: To reduce the sharpness or intensity of something.
keyTerms.example: Headphones cut the sharp edges of a noisy room.

comprehension.prompt: What did the experiment from the nineties find?
options: Noise helped with simple, repetitive tasks and hurt tasks that needed thinking.
comprehension.explanation: The noisy group did better on dull tasks and much worse on tasks that needed thought.

comprehension.prompt: According to the episode, why do headphones help even with no music playing?
options: They cut the sharp edges of the noise.
They make you work faster by hiding your screen.
comprehension.explanation: “Even headphones with no music playing will cut the sharp edges.”

comprehension.prompt: Why is it good to have a different sound for studying and for resting?
options: Because if not, you stop learning what that sound means.
Because sentences are shorter with noise.
Because your brain forgets sounds after two weeks.
comprehension.explanation: “If the same music plays while you write and while you rest, you stop learning what it means.”

data.title: Things you learn on the metro
data.summary: An episode about the metro as a surprise classroom: the words you only learn when you travel every day, and why a sentence you hear on a platform is easier to remember than one in a textbook.

segments.speaker: Andrés
segments.text: Welcome to Cosas del Metro. I am Andrés, and this week: the words you only learn when you travel. Every day, for a year, on the same line.

segments.speaker: Andrés
segments.text: Nobody teaches you the vocabulary of a station. You learn it because you need it. The announcement says the name of the next station and you want to know whether you have to get up now or two stops later.

segments.speaker: Andrés
segments.text: So you learn 'the next stop'. You learn 'the last stop', because the driver says it at the end of the line and you finally know where you are. You learn 'connection', which in English is 'transfer'.

segments.speaker: Andrés
segments.text: And you learn the small politeness of a shared space. 'Excuse me.' 'Sorry, is this seat taken?' You learn them standing up, with your bag on your shoulder, and they stick in a way that a classroom sentence never does.

segments.speaker: Andrés
segments.text: Then there is the vocabulary of delay. When the line stops for four minutes with no announcement, people look around. And then somebody says, in a voice that is not really a question: 'Is it running?'

segments.speaker: Andrés
segments.text: Four words, one grammatical mistake, and a completely different meaning. 'Is it running' means 'is it moving again'. 'Is it running' does not mean 'is the service operating'. In English, a small wrong word can change the whole question.

segments.speaker: Andrés
segments.text: I do not think teachers should stop using textbooks. But I do think a language is also the set of words a city hands you for free, every morning, whether you are ready or not.

segments.speaker: Andrés
segments.text: So the exercise for this week is simple. On your next trip, write down ten words you did not know on Monday. Ten is enough. Then use five of them badly tonight, in a sentence about your day.

keyTerms.definition: The station that comes immediately after the one you are at.
keyTerms.example: The next stop is where you have to change.

keyTerms.definition: To change from one line or vehicle to another during a journey.
A period of time when something happens later than expected.
keyTerms.example: There was a ten-minute delay on the line.

comprehension.prompt: According to Andrés, why do we learn station vocabulary so easily?
options: Because we need it, every single day.
Because it is written on the walls.
comprehension.explanation: “Nobody teaches you the vocabulary of a station. You learn it because you need it.”

comprehension.prompt: What does 'Is it running?' mean in the episode?
comprehension.explanation: In the episode, 'Is it running?' means “Is it moving again?”, not “Is the service operating?”.

comprehension.prompt: What is the exercise for this week?
options: Write down ten new words and use five of them, even if you make mistakes.
Listen to the episode five times.
comprehension.explanation: “Write down ten words you did not know on Monday... Then use five of them badly tonight, in a sentence about your day.”

data.title: The Last Tram
data.summary: The last tram of the night goes down a street where nobody gets off. A 4-minute short film about the hours when a city becomes quiet and empty.

scenes.speaker: Narrator
scenes.line: The last tram leaves the square at eleven forty.
scenes.translation: El último tranvía sale de la plaza a las once y cuarenta.

scenes.speaker: Narrator
scenes.line: By then the shops have closed and the square belongs to the people who have nowhere else to be.
scenes.translation: Para entonces las tiendas han cerrado y la plaza es de quienes no tienen otro sitio donde estar.

scenes.speaker: Old man
scenes.line: You are the last one?
scenes.translation: ¿Usted es el último?

scenes.speaker: Driver
scenes.line: I am the last one.
scenes.translation: Soy el último.

scenes.speaker: Old man
scenes.line: Then I will wait for you.
scenes.translation: Entonces lo espero a usted.

scenes.speaker: Narrator
scenes.line: He says it as if it were obvious. As if waiting for a tram at midnight were a thing that people did every night of their lives.
scenes.translation: Lo dice como si fuera obvio. Como si esperar un tranvía a medianoche fuera algo que la gente hiciera todas las noches de su vida.

scenes.speaker: Driver
scenes.line: You will be here when I come back.
scenes.translation: Usted estará aquí cuando yo vuelva.

scenes.speaker: Old man
scenes.line: I will be here when you come back.
scenes.translation: Estaré aquí cuando usted vuelva.

scenes.speaker: Narrator
scenes.line: The doors close. The tram takes the square, and the two of them watch each other through the glass.
scenes.translation: Las puertas se cierran. El tranvía cruza la plaza y los dos se miran a través del vidrio.

scenes.speaker: Narrator
scenes.line: The square is empty again. But something in it has changed, and nobody will say what.
scenes.translation: La plaza vuelve a estar vacía. Pero algo en ella ha cambiado, y nadie dirá qué.

comprehension.prompt: What time does the last tram leave?
comprehension.explanation: The narrator starts with "The last tram leaves the square at eleven forty."

comprehension.prompt: What does the old man say when the driver says he is the last one?
comprehension.explanation: The dialogue is: "You are the last one?" / "I am the last one." / "Then I will wait for you."

comprehension.prompt: What has changed at the end?
options: The square is empty, and nothing else.
The tram comes back with more passengers.
Something in the square has changed, but nobody can say what.
comprehension.explanation: «The square is empty again. But something in it has changed, and nobody will say what.»

data.title: Paper and Ink
data.summary: In a bookbinder's workshop, a man tries to write a letter he never sends. A short film about the gap between what we say and what we write.

scenes.speaker: Narrator
scenes.line: He has been coming to the workshop for eleven years. He brings the same book every time.
scenes.translation: Lleva once años viniendo al taller. Trae siempre el mismo libro.

scenes.speaker: Narrator
scenes.line: The book is called A Handbook of Correspondence. It was printed in nineteen fifty-four, and it is still, according to the owner, the only book about the subject that has ever been written.
scenes.translation: El libro se titula Manual de correspondencia. Se imprimió en mil novecientos cincuenta y cuatro y sigue siendo, según el dueño, el único libro sobre el tema que se ha escrito.

scenes.speaker: Binder
scenes.line: Ninety-one pages. Fifty-one of them are about envelopes.
scenes.translation: Noventa y una páginas. Cincuenta y una son sobre sobres.

scenes.speaker: Man
scenes.line: Envelopes are the difficult part. Paper is easy.
scenes.translation: Los sobres son la parte difícil. El papel es fácil.

scenes.speaker: Binder
scenes.line: You are not writing a letter. You are choosing a letter.
scenes.translation: Usted no está escribiendo una carta. Está eligiendo una carta.

scenes.speaker: Narrator
scenes.line: He says this without any weight. Then he looks at the book for a while, and corrects himself.
scenes.translation: Lo dice sin ninguna ironía. Luego mira el libro un rato y se corrige.

scenes.speaker: Man
scenes.line: You are not choosing a letter. You are choosing not to send one.
scenes.translation: Usted no está eligiendo una carta. Está eligiendo no enviar ninguna.

scenes.speaker: Narrator
scenes.line: The binder does not answer. She ties the pages, trims the edges, and sets the book on the shelf with the others, where it will wait.
scenes.translation: La encuadernadora no contesta. Ata las páginas, recorta los bordes y pone el libro en la estantería con los demás, donde esperará.

scenes.speaker: Narrator
scenes.line: He will be back on Thursday. He will bring the same book.
scenes.translation: Volverá el jueves. Traerá el mismo libro.

comprehension.prompt: How much of the handbook is about envelopes?
comprehension.explanation: "Ninety-one pages. Fifty-one of them are about envelopes." Fifty-one out of ninety-one is a little more than half.

comprehension.prompt: What does the man finally say he is choosing?
comprehension.explanation: «You are not choosing a letter. You are choosing not to send one.»

comprehension.prompt: What happens to the book at the end?
options: The bookbinder puts it on the shelf.
She gives it back without binding it.
comprehension.explanation: The bookbinder puts it on the shelf with the others, where it will wait.

data.title: Night Shift at the Observatory
data.summary: An astronomer alone in an observatory on a January night, talking to a radio that will never answer.

scenes.speaker: Narrator
scenes.line: The dome opens at sunset and closes at sunrise, and between those two events the observatory belongs to whoever is on shift.
scenes.translation: La cúpula se abre al atardecer y se cierra al amanecer, y entre esos dos hechos el observatorio pertenece a quien esté de turno.

scenes.speaker: Dr. Reyes
scenes.line: Meridian transit in forty minutes. Coffee number two is wrong, by the way. Somebody left the sugar out.
scenes.translation: Tránsito meridiano en cuarenta minutos. Por cierto, el café número dos está mal. Alguien dejó el azúcar fuera.

scenes.speaker: Narrator
scenes.line: Nobody answers. The radio on the desk is tuned to a frequency that stopped transmitting in nineteen ninety-eight, and she keeps it on because the static is easier to work with than silence.
scenes.translation: Nadie contesta. La radio del escritorio está sintonizada a una frecuencia que dejó de transmitir en mil novecientos noventa y ocho, y ella la deja encendida porque la estática es más fácil de trabajar que el silencio.

scenes.speaker: Dr. Reyes
scenes.line: Are you there?
scenes.translation: ¿Está ahí?

scenes.speaker: Narrator
scenes.line: The static does not answer either. But she asks again, and then again, because the question is not really for the radio.
scenes.translation: La estática tampoco contesta. Pero pregunta otra vez, y luego otra, porque la pregunta no es realmente para la radio.

scenes.speaker: Dr. Reyes
scenes.line: The plate is finished. One hundred and two exposures. It is the clearest night of the year so far, and there is nobody here to see it with.
scenes.translation: La placa está terminada. Ciento dos exposiciones. Es la noche más clara del año hasta ahora, y no hay nadie aquí para verlo con ella.

scenes.speaker: Narrator
scenes.line: She closes the dome at sunrise. It takes forty minutes and she does it alone, as she has done for six years.
scenes.translation: Cierra la cúpula al amanecer. Tarda cuarenta minutos y lo hace sola, como lleva haciendo seis años.

scenes.speaker: Dr. Reyes
scenes.line: Same frequency tomorrow?
scenes.translation: ¿Misma frecuencia mañana?

scenes.speaker: Narrator
scenes.line: The static keeps its shape. It is the only company that has never needed her to explain why she is still awake.
scenes.translation: La estática mantiene su forma. Es la única compañía que nunca ha necesitado que le explique por qué sigue despierta.

comprehension.prompt: Why does Dr. Reyes leave the radio on, even though nobody answers?
options: Because it works as an alarm clock.
Because the static is easier to work with than silence.
Because she is waiting for an urgent message.
Because she does not know how to turn it off.
comprehension.explanation: «The static is easier to work with than silence.»

comprehension.prompt: How many exposures does the plate have?
comprehension.explanation: «One hundred and two exposures.»

comprehension.prompt: What does the narrator say about her question to the radio?
options: That the question is for the radio.
That the question is not really for the radio.
That the radio will finally answer.
That the question is an observatory rule.
comprehension.explanation: «The question is not really for the radio.»

questions.prompt: What was the difference between the two boxes?
options: One held letters from her husband and the other from Mara.

questions.explanation: The last paragraph tells us about these two times.

passage: Elena wrote her first letter when she was seventeen, and she never sent it. She wrote almost every week for thirty years, and she kept them in a banana box under her bed. She wrote on the backs of the delivery calendars from the shop on the corner, because paper cost money and her mother kept the calendars to wrap things in.

In 1994 the letter said: “Mara, today a man came to the house to ask for my hand and I said no. I do not know why I said no. Write and tell me if that was foolish.” By the time she was ready to send it, six months had passed and the question had become strange.

By the year thirty she had filled two boxes. The first held the years when she still believed she would send them. The second held the years when sending them had become a way of talking about herself.

options: White like snow in the morning.

questions.prompt: What happened with the first step on the ice?
options: It was easy, and the second was frightening.

questions.explanation: “He stepped out. The first step was frightening. The second was not.”

passage: On Thursday night the air was so still that the dogs did not bark. Tomás woke because the house was cold in a new way, and because he heard a sound he had never heard before: a long, thin crack, like a plate breaking in another room.
He went to the window. The river was white. Not white the way clouds are white, but white the way metal is white, and it was making that sound all along its length, from the bridge to the bend.

In the afternoon Tomás took his father's old skates and walked down to the bank. The ice was covered in a thin layer of snow, and where his foot landed the snow went under and the ice made a deep green sound under it, like a door. He stepped out. The first step was frightening. The second was not.
